title: Is Venezuela Moving Toward Democracy?
gist: Nine months after Maduro's capture, CSIS judges the US 'regime management' plan has completed stabilization under acting president Delcy Rodríguez and opened Venezuela's oil sector (100-year concessions over 17 fields with ~65B barrels; Chevron $7B+ JV plans), but daily life remains dire (534% inflation) and no electoral timetable exists. The core risk is that stabilization becomes permanent as oil deals create constituencies against elections that could overturn their terms.

insights.claim: After Maduro's January 3, 2026 capture, the US chose a regime-management strategy, keeping Delcy Rodríguez as acting president and most military and security structures in place, rather than installing opposition leader María Corina Machado.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Continuity of the Chavista apparatus defines who investors deal with in Venezuela.
insights.quote: The phases outline an administration that did not pursue regime change but rather adopted a regime management strategy
insights.locator: After the capture of Nicolás Maduro

insights.claim: Stabilization succeeded by avoiding an intra-regime rupture: Rodríguez removed Defense Minister Padrino López after nearly 12 years and Alex Saab was handed to the US without organized backlash.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reduced near-term political violence risk supports oil-sector operational continuity.
insights.quote: An important but underappreciated element of Venezuela’s stabilization has been the avoidance of an intra-regime rupture.

insights.claim: Rodríguez has used eight months to consolidate power, replacing military leadership and installing loyalists across ministries while retaining Maduro-era institutional architecture.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: An entrenched interim leader raises the odds of a durable non-democratic order.
insights.quote: She has rebuilt the state around herself, replacing military leadership and installing her own people across ministries

insights.claim: Venezuela's amended hydrocarbons law of January 29 introduced public-private partnerships with less state control and lower royalties, and US Treasury OFAC lifted specific restrictions to let US companies trade Venezuelan crude.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Opens Venezuelan crude to US traders and refiners, increasing heavy sour supply.
insights.quote: public-private partnership agreements with less state control and lower royalties

insights.claim: The US-Rodríguez oil deal grants 100-year concessions over 17 oil fields holding some 65 billion barrels.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A large potential reserve base opens to US companies, with long-run supply implications for oil markets.
insights.quote: 100-year concessions over 17 oil fields holding some 65 billion barrels
insights.locator: Some progress has been made toward

insights.claim: Chevron plans to invest over $7 billion over five years in joint ventures, ExxonMobil, whose CEO once called Venezuela 'uninvestable', is reportedly near a preliminary deal, and at least one other US oil company is set to announce a deal.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US majors re-entering Venezuela signals capex and production upside, and exposure to political risk.
insights.quote: Chevron followed with a separate announcement on joint venture plans to invest over $7 billion over the next five years
insights.locator: Some progress has been made toward

insights.claim: The August oil agreement appears to contradict the amended hydrocarbons law capping oil contracts at 25 years and may conflict with Venezuela's constitution.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Legal fragility means a future democratic government could challenge the concessions, a key tail risk for investors.
insights.quote: The agreement signed in August already seems to contradict the amended hydrocarbons law that caps oil contracts at 25 years and may conflict with the country’s constitution.
insights.locator: The oil deal between the regime

insights.claim: Parties benefiting from the oil deal have incentives to protect the system that produced it and avoid an election that might overturn its terms; Trump said 'Venezuela is making a tremendous amount of money, so are we.'
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Commercial interests may delay democratization, prolonging political risk around asset legitimacy.
insights.quote: Parties benefiting from the deal have reason to protect the system that produced it, and to avoid an election that could lead to a future democratic government overturning its terms.
insights.locator: The disagreement is not over the goal

insights.claim: Economic normalization strengthens US leverage over Caracas in the short term but creates constituencies for stability that raise the political and financial cost of using that leverage later, so leverage has a shelf life.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US pressure for elections likely weakens as investment grows; time-sensitive political catalyst.
insights.quote: Economic normalization could therefore strengthen U.S. leverage over Caracas in the short term while gradually increasing the political and financial costs of using that leverage later.

insights.claim: An electoral calendar with milestones such as National Electoral Council reform and voter roll updates would give investors greater clarity about the political environment for long-term commitments.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: An election timetable would be a de-risking catalyst for long-dated Venezuela investments.
insights.quote: It would also give investors greater clarity about the political environment in which long-term commitments are being made.

insights.claim: Venezuelan inflation slowed to 8.9% month-on-month in August from 19.9% the prior month but still ran at 534.2% year over year, the minimum wage frozen since 2022 covers under 1% of monthly family food costs, and 9 in 10 households suffer power cuts.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Macro stabilization lags the oil opening; domestic consumption and power reliability remain weak.
insights.quote: Inflation, which slowed to 8.9 percent in August from 19.9 percent the previous ‌month, is still running at 534.2 percent, year over year.
insights.locator: Even as steps are being taken

insights.claim: The June 24 double earthquakes left over 6,100 dead, about 1.8 million needing assistance and over $19 billion in direct physical damage, likely delaying the political transition.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Large reconstruction needs and delayed transition timeline.
insights.quote: which left over 6,100 dead, about 1.8 million people needing assistance, and over $19 billion in direct physical damage

insights.claim: Regime and opposition negotiators agreed to jointly pursue recovery of 31 metric tons of Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England, with part of the proceeds for earthquake reconstruction.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Potential unlocking of frozen sovereign gold reserves is a notable sovereign-asset development.
insights.quote: specifically, 31 metric tons of gold held at the Bank of England

insights.claim: Negotiations between Jorge Rodríguez and opposition leader Dinorah Figuera produced a TSJ reform, but critics argue it does not really reduce legislative control over judicial appointments, and electoral council restructuring and voter rolls have not been addressed.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Institutional reforms are largely cosmetic so far; rule-of-law risk persists for contracts.
insights.quote: changing who sits on the court is not the same as changing what the court does
insights.locator: A more hopeful development is that

insights.claim: Holding regional and parliamentary elections before a presidential vote would let Rodríguez show an electoral opening without risking her job, divide the opposition and delay a true transition.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch election sequencing as a signal of whether the transition is real or stalled.
insights.quote: it would create competition within opposition forces and inevitably delay a true transition in the country
insights.locator: Given President Trump’s position on the issue

insights.claim: The opposition is split on sequencing: Figuera pursues reform through existing regime institutions while economic recovery proceeds, whereas Machado insists presidential elections come first and that no investment deal can hold without rule of law.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Opposition division reduces pressure for elections and complicates assessment of contract durability.
insights.quote: Figuera has bet that economic recovery and institutional reform can proceed while the electoral question stays open; Machado holds the contrary.
insights.locator: The disagreement is not over the goal

insights.claim: Trump and Rubio diverge: Trump praises Rodríguez and prioritizes economic gains, while Rubio says elections should follow electoral council reform; Rodríguez will exploit these tensions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Mixed US signals raise uncertainty about policy continuity toward Venezuela.
insights.quote: President Trump and Secretary Rubio seem to be moving at slightly different speeds.

insights.claim: The greatest US challenge may no longer be stabilizing Venezuela but preventing the stabilization phase from becoming a permanent, durable non-democratic order.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A permanent interim regime implies long-run legitimacy and expropriation risk for investments.
insights.quote: the greatest challenge facing the United States may no longer be stabilizing Venezuela but preventing the stabilization phase from becoming permanent
